transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me, I really appreciate it. 

Um, well, I guess the main reason I’m here is... and I hope I explain this okay... I manage health services, and I'm usually very dedicated to my job, I promise. But I've been having a little bit of trouble. It’s just that anything that takes real, sitting-down brain work—like putting together my monthly reports or, say, planning a big multi-site health event—it just feels like I hit a wall. 

I end up putting it off, even when I know it really matters for my team and the clinics. It’s a bit embarrassing to admit, honestly, because I really do care about my work and I know I should just push through it. Am I making sense so far? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.

Can you tell me if this difficulty concentrating or putting off tasks happens only at work, or does it also affect you in other areas of your life, like at home or with friends? And when you mention feeling this way, do you also feel down, sad, or hopeless during these times?

Oh, that’s a really good question. Um... I wouldn't say I feel sad or hopeless, no. I'm generally a pretty positive guy! I do get a little frustrated with myself, though. 

As for where it happens... well, it’s not *just* work, I suppose. I mean, I’m still getting by at the clinics and in my community, so it’s not a total disaster or anything. I really don't want to make it sound worse than it is. But... I guess if I'm being completely honest, some deadlines have slipped. And, um, people have had to cover gaps for me sometimes. My team is incredibly supportive, but I feel terrible when they have to do that. 

And it does happen with my friends, too. I’ve actually embarrassed myself more than a few times lately with these... well, these last-minute apologies to coworkers and friends because I just didn't get around to doing what I said I would or I left things too late. It’s not how I want people to see me, you know? 

Am I explaining that clearly enough for you? I just want to make sure I'm answering exactly what you're asking.
Do you often feel restless, as if you can't sit still, or do you find yourself doing things very quickly without thinking them through?

Oh, no, I don't think I struggle with that at all. Um, I can sit still just fine. I actually have to sit through a lot of long administrative meetings for the clinics, and I'm usually perfectly quiet for those. I certainly don't feel like I'm bouncing off the walls or anything like that. 

And as for doing things without thinking... no, I wouldn't say so. If anything, I'm probably the opposite? Like, I might delay starting a project, but I don't rush into things blindly. I always try to be really careful and thoughtful about my decisions, because I know my staff is relying on me to be steady. 

Does that answer your question okay? I just want to make sure I'm staying on track for you and giving you the right picture.
Have you noticed that you're not enjoying activities as much as you used to, or that things you normally look forward to don't feel as rewarding?

No, I wouldn't say that at all, actually. I still really enjoy the things I've always liked. I love spending time with my friends, and I still get a lot of satisfaction out of the good moments at work, like when we have a successful community health drive. 

I don't feel numb to things or anything like that. I still look forward to the weekend and my hobbies. It's really just that... well, that trouble getting started on the tedious stuff that I mentioned before. But my actual enjoyment of life is still very much there, I promise. 

Is that what you were looking for? I hope I'm not over-explaining, I just want to be sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to figure this out.
Do you find yourself getting easily distracted by things around you, even when you're trying to focus on something important?

Well, um... I guess maybe a little bit? I mean, I really do try my best to pay attention, especially when it's important. I know how crucial it is to stay focused. 

But sometimes... like, if we're in a meeting and someone's giving a budget update, I might get a little sidetracked. It’s not that I don’t care! It’s just that, you know, if a phone vibrates across the table, or I hear people talking out in the hallway, my attention just sort of drifts over to that. Or even just a random thought pops into my head, like something I forgot to do for my bowling league, and suddenly I realize I've missed the last few minutes of what was being said. 

I always try to catch up right away, though, and I really hope it doesn't make me look unprofessional. I don't want people to think I'm ignoring them. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not making it sound like I'm completely incapable of paying attention, because I really do try hard to be present.
When did you first start noticing these difficulties with focus and getting started on tasks? Were they something you experienced even as a child, or did they begin more recently in adulthood?

Well, um... I guess it's not exactly a new thing. I mean, I don't want to make it sound like I was a terrible student or anything, because I really wasn't! My teachers always said I was bright. 

But, um, even back in elementary school, they would tell my parents that I was... well, daydreaming a lot. And I guess I had a bit of a habit of losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in my homework. It wasn't that I didn't want to do it, I just... things would slip my mind. My mom actually had to check my backpack every night just to make sure things got turned in. 

I really tried my best, though, and I got through school okay. I just... I suppose this has been a bit of a lifelong quirk for me. I hope that's the kind of information you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline so you can get the full picture.
Have you ever found yourself acting on impulse, doing things without really thinking about the consequences first?

Oh, no, not really. I mean, I'm a pretty careful person, especially with my job. As a health services manager, you really have to think things through, right? You can't just make snap decisions when it comes to budgets or staffing. 

I really try to be thoughtful about what I do. I don't... I don't just jump into things or blurt things out without thinking. I like to have a plan. I mean, sure, everyone makes a hasty decision at the grocery store now and then, but nothing serious. I've always been pretty level-headed that way. 

Is that what you mean by impulsive? I just want to make sure I'm not misunderstanding the question, because I really don't want to give you the wrong idea about how I handle things.
Can you tell me if your difficulties with focus and starting tasks happen in different settings, like at home or in social situations, or are they mostly limited to work-related tasks?

Well, um... I guess it happens a little bit everywhere? But I really try not to let it affect my home life or my friends. I mean, at work, it's a bit more obvious because of the paperwork and the deadlines, like I mentioned. 

At home, it's... well, maybe I'm a little slow to get around to things like organizing the garage or sorting through the mail. My wife might say I leave little piles of things around the house, but I always intend to get back to them! I really do. And socially, I guess sometimes I might drift off a tiny bit if a conversation goes on for a really long time, but I always smile and nod, and I try so hard to be a good listener. I don't want anyone to think I don't care about what they're saying. 

So, I suppose it's not just at work, but I really try my best to manage it so it doesn't bother anyone else. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it right, I just don't want you to think I'm completely disorganized in every part of my life.

Have you ever felt an internal sense of restlessness, like you can't relax even when you want to, or found yourself needing to get up and move around during times when you’re supposed to stay still, like when you're reading or trying to wind down at the end of the day?

Um, no, I wouldn't really say I experience that. Actually, sitting still is... well, it's something I'm perfectly fine with. After a long day at work, I'm usually more than happy to just sink into the couch and stay put for the evening. 

I don't really get that... that physical urge to jump up or pace around. I can physically relax just fine. I mean, sure, sometimes I might tap my foot if I'm listening to a good song or something, but nothing at all like what you're describing. I definitely don't feel antsy or restless inside. 

I hope it's okay that I don't have that issue? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the exact right information and not leaving anything out. Does that help answer your question?

Can you tell me more about your childhood experiences with staying on task or completing schoolwork? Did you often struggle to follow through on instructions or finish things you started, even when you understood what needed to be done?

Well, um... I guess school was always a little tricky for me, even way back in elementary school. But I wasn't a bad kid! I really wasn't. My teachers always told my parents that I was bright and capable. They were always very nice about it.

It's just that... well, I suppose I had a bit of a habit of daydreaming. I'd be looking out the window, just sort of lost in my own thoughts, and maybe miss a direction or two. And, um, I guess I wasn't the best at keeping track of things. I'd lose worksheets, or I'd do the homework and then just completely forget to turn it in. 

Honestly, if my mother hadn't checked my backpack every single night to make sure things were where they needed to be, I probably would have missed a lot more assignments. She was a huge help. But I always understood the work! I really did. I just... struggled a bit with the follow-through part, I suppose. 

Is that the kind of thing you're looking for? I hope I'm not making myself sound like I was a terrible student. I really did try hard to please my teachers and my parents.
Can you tell me if these difficulties with focus and follow-through have ever significantly affected your performance in school, your work, or your relationships with others?

Well, um... I really wouldn't say it's ruined anything, you know? I'm still getting by at work, and I still have a good life and friends. I'm a medical services manager, which is a lot of responsibility, so I really do my best to keep everything running smoothly. 

I guess... well, there have been a few times where things slipped a little bit. Like, maybe a deadline got pushed back, or someone had to step in and help me cover a gap because I got a little behind. I always feel terrible when that happens, and I always make sure to apologize right away! I've definitely had to send a few embarrassing last-minute apology emails to coworkers, or even to friends if I forgot to RSVP or lost track of a plan we made. 

But I always try to make up for it, and people are usually really understanding. I just don't want to be a burden on anyone. Does that make sense? I hope that doesn't sound too bad. I really am trying my hardest to keep everything together.

Can you tell me if these difficulties have caused significant problems in your life—like lower performance in school or work, trouble meeting responsibilities at home, or issues with friends or family members?

Um, well, I guess I sort of touched on that just now, but... I really wouldn't use the word "significant," you know? Like I mentioned, there are those little slips at work or a missed RSVP here and there, but nothing major. I haven't been fired or anything terrible like that! I'm very dedicated to my job. 

As for at home... well, my wife is really wonderful and she handles a lot of the household organizing and the bills, so I don't really have the chance to mess too much up there. I try to be as helpful as I possibly can with the chores she gives me, though! I really do. 

So, no, no huge, life-altering problems. I hope that makes sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture, and I wouldn't want you to think things are worse than they actually are. Did I answer that okay?

Can you tell me if your difficulty staying focused and following through on tasks happens in different parts of your life—like at home, in social situations, or when you're doing something you enjoy—or does it only seem to come up in certain places, like at work?

Um, well, I guess it's a little bit of everywhere, but I really don't think it's too noticeable. Like I said, my wife handles a lot of the big things at home, so I'm mostly just following her lead there. If she asks me to do something, I really try to get it done right away so I don't forget. 

And, um, with friends or hobbies... I suppose my mind wanders sometimes when we're just sitting around talking, or if I'm trying to read a book for fun, I might have to read the same page a couple of times. But that's pretty normal, right? Everyone gets a little distracted when they're relaxing. 

I definitely wouldn't say it's a huge problem in any one place. It's just sort of... a background thing, I guess? I really hope I'm explaining this well. I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need without making it sound like I can't function or anything. Is that helpful?
Have you ever felt an inner sense of restlessness, like your mind is always going, even if you're not physically moving around?

Um, restlessness? I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, my mind is definitely busy, but I feel like that's just because I have a lot going on with work and trying to make sure I'm doing a good job for everyone. 

I wouldn't say I feel like I'm always going or anything like that. I'm actually pretty good at just sitting quietly, especially when my wife and I are watching TV in the evenings. I might be thinking about what I need to do the next day, but I wouldn't call it an inner restlessness. It's just normal planning, you know? 

I really don't feel physically antsy or anything. I hope that's the right kind of answer? I just don't want to make it sound like I'm bouncing off the walls inside my head when I'm really just trying to be responsible. Does that make sense?
Have you ever felt the need to constantly keep your hands or feet moving, even when you're trying to sit still, like during a meeting or while watching a movie?

Oh, um, no, definitely not. I'm actually very good at sitting still. In my role—managing the staff and everything—I really have to maintain a professional presence during meetings, so I definitely don't fidget or move around constantly. 

I mean, I might cross my legs or adjust my posture if I get stiff, just like anyone else would, but I'm really not disruptive at all. I don't have that urge to keep my hands or feet moving, even if it's a long meeting or a long movie. 

I hope that's what you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm being helpful and giving you the right answers. Did I explain that okay?
